analysis.one_liner: Repeals tax deductions and credits that subsidize oil and gas production.
analysis.headline: The End Oil and Gas Tax Subsidies Act was introduced by Rep. Casten with 16 Democratic cosponsors in January 2025 and has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or a vote ever since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end a long list of special tax breaks for oil and gas companies, including credits for marginal wells and enhanced oil recovery, the deduction for intangible drilling costs, percentage depletion, and a deduction for tertiary injectants. It would stop major integrated oil companies from using last-in, first-out inventory accounting, block oil and gas businesses from the qualified business income deduction, tighten the foreign tax credit for companies paying levies to foreign governments that give them a benefit in return, and expand the excise tax on imported crude to cover tar sands and oil shale products. Supporters frame this as ending subsidies that cost taxpayers money and tilt the playing field against cleaner energy.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, because the money now lost to oil and gas tax breaks would instead be collected as revenue. Clean energy producers would also benefit from a more level playing field, since oil and gas would no longer receive tax preferences that renewable sources never had.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers and clean energy producers

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the credits for producing oil and gas from marginal wells and for enhanced oil recovery, along with the deductions for intangible drilling costs, tertiary injectants, and percentage depletion, ending tax preferences unique to the oil and gas industry.
It denies the qualified business income deduction to oil and gas production, refining, processing, transportation, and distribution activities, closing a break those businesses currently claim.

It prohibits major integrated oil companies from using LIFO accounting and stretches the write-off period for geological and geophysical expenses from two years to seven, delaying deductions and reducing their present value.

It extends the federal excise tax on imported petroleum to oil from tar sands and oil shale, which currently escapes the tax that funds oil spill response, and gives the Treasury authority to cover similar new petroleum products.

It limits the foreign tax credit for companies paying levies to foreign governments that also grant them a specific economic benefit, so payments that function as kickbacks for extraction rights can no longer be credited against U.S. taxes.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, particularly independent producers and operators of marginal wells who rely on percentage depletion and the marginal well credit, and major integrated oil companies that use LIFO accounting. Any added tax cost could be passed to consumers through fuel prices at the margin.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies and independent producers

drawbacks.text: Opponents of ending these provisions argue that stripping deductions and credits raises the cost of domestic production, which could reduce output, shrink supply, and push fuel prices up for consumers at a time when energy costs are already a household burden. Small operators of marginal 'stripper' wells, which are already barely profitable, would be hit hardest and some wells could shut down sooner.

The changes take effect for taxable years after December 31, 2024, so companies with projects underway would face higher tax bills on existing investment plans, an abrupt change for businesses that planned around the current rules.

The bill is a narrow revenue and tax-equity measure; it does not directly lower any consumer's costs, and its benefits to households come only indirectly, through whatever Congress eventually does with the revenue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: taxpayers stop paying for tax breaks that only oil and gas producers can use, while the industry absorbs a higher effective tax rate. The strongest honest objection is the marginal-well provision — small operators, not the majors, depend most on percentage depletion and the marginal well credit, and ending those could retire some marginal wells early, slightly tightening supply. Against that, the same repeal removes preferences that have no equivalent in any other industry and that keep oil and gas artificially cheap to produce relative to cleaner alternatives. The foreign tax credit fix is hard to defend on the merits: it stops companies from crediting foreign levies that function as payments for extraction privileges.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has never taken it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Sean Casten introduced the bill on January 14, 2025, joined by 16 Democratic cosponsors; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored it.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on January 14, 2025, which is the only action recorded since introduction.
The Ways and Means Committee has held no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, and it has not been scheduled for floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies, which keep the tax deductions and credits the bill would have repealed, because the bill never left committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies keep their tax breaks

for.name: Rep. Sean Casten
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Oil and Gas Tax Subsidies Act of 2025 in the House.

for.name: 16 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on January 14, 2025 and has taken no action on it since — no hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 original supporters are House Democrats; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored, and with Republicans holding 223 of 440 House seats and the Ways and Means chairmanship, the bill has had no path to the floor.

industries.note: The bill repeals a suite of tax preferences used only by this industry — percentage depletion, intangible drilling cost expensing, marginal well and enhanced oil recovery credits, tertiary injectant deductions, and the QBI deduction — raising its effective tax rate. The industry's gain under current law comes at taxpayer expense, so its interest in keeping the status quo runs against the public's.

Small operators depend most on percentage depletion and the marginal well credit, so the repeal bites them harder than the majors. The industry position keeps taxpayer-funded preferences in place that the public pays for.

The bill bars companies producing at least 500,000 barrels a day with over $1 billion in receipts from LIFO accounting, which front-loads inventory deductions, and limits their foreign tax credit for levies tied to extraction benefits abroad. These are timing and credit rules that let the largest firms pay less tax than their reported economics suggest.

industries.industry: Tar sands and oil shale importers
industries.note: The bill redefines crude oil for excise tax purposes to include bitumen and kerogen-derived oil, subjecting imports that currently escape the tax — which funds oil spill liability — to the same levy as conventional crude. Closing the loophole spreads the funding of oil spill response onto the imports that create the risk.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding a 223-seat House majority and the Ways and Means chairmanship, and zero Republican support, the bill is very unlikely to advance. Its most probable end is dying quietly in committee at the close of the 119th Congress, the way prior versions of oil and gas subsidy repeal have; it could resurface if Democrats win the chamber in 2026, and some provisions resemble proposals that appear in broader tax or energy packages.
